title: Decently and in order (1 Corinthians 14)
hook: gifts in worship must build others up, and God is not the author of confusion
tomorrow: if you could keep only four lines, which four would they be?

segments.voice: Yesterday's word: one body, every part needed. Today, what happens when every part wants to talk at once.

A group chat at full speed: three plans, two polls, a voice memo, someone typing in all caps. Everyone has something to add, and nobody can follow. Worship at Corinth sounded like that. "When ye come together, every one of you hath a psalm, hath a doctrine, hath a tongue, hath a revelation, hath an interpretation." Paul pictures an outsider walking in on several people speaking in tongues at once, and asks, "will they not say that ye are mad?" So what does he tell them?
screen: `THE GROUP CHAT AT FULL SPEED.` → `EVERY ONE OF YOU HATH A PSALM.` → `WILL THEY NOT SAY YE ARE MAD?`

segments.voice: Not to stop. To build. His test for every gift is one word: edify, build up. "He that speaketh in an unknown tongue edifieth himself; but he that prophesieth edifieth the church." He isn't against tongues; "I speak with tongues," he says. But in church, "I had rather speak five words with my understanding, that by my voice I might teach others also, than ten thousand words in an unknown tongue." Then a picture from the battlefield: "if the trumpet give an uncertain sound, who shall prepare himself to the battle?" He wants both at once: "I will pray with the spirit, and I will pray with the understanding also." So, practical rules. Tongues by two or three, in turn, with someone to interpret. Prophets one at a time, so all can learn. Why? "For God is not the author of confusion, but of peace." The summary: "Let all things be done unto edifying." And the chapter's last words: "Let all things be done decently and in order." Order here isn't stiffness. It's what lets the newcomer at the back follow along. Churches today read this chapter differently: some pray in tongues in worship, and others believe those gifts belonged to the early church. Paul's test stands between them: does it build the others up?
screen: `EDIFY: BUILD UP.` · `FIVE WORDS WITH MY UNDERSTANDING.` · `ONE AT A TIME, SO ALL CAN LEARN.` · `NOT THE AUTHOR OF CONFUSION.` · then, large: `ALL THINGS EDIFY.`

segments.voice: Say one line out loud, slowly, the way you'd say it so a stranger could follow. If you pray, it can be a line you already pray, with the spirit and with the understanding; if not, any line you mean, like a word of thanks. Then sit with what it was like to say it for someone else's ears.
Decently and in order. Paul's rule for worship full of gifts: take turns, speak so others understand, and build everyone up.
Keep this one: all things edify, every gift pointed at the people in the room. That's the day.

howItsDone: In Pentecostal and charismatic churches, people pray in tongues in worship and look for an interpretation, as this chapter describes; other churches read it as a call for worship that is clear and builds everyone up.

fork.setup: your small group's sharing time keeps running long: two people talk most of the hour, and the newcomers never speak. what fits Paul's chapter?

fork.reveal: Paul's rule: prophets one at a time, that all may learn. order isn't silence; it's room for everyone to be built up.

notes: The index carry is 'all things edify'; the KJV of 14:26 reads 'Let all things be done unto edifying'. The lesson quotes the KJV and keeps the carry as the index has it.
The lesson does not treat 14:34–35 (women keeping silence in the churches), which churches read in very different ways. A scholar should decide whether the lesson needs to name it.
'Others believe those gifts belonged to the early church' describes cessationist readings without naming or ranking them; howItsDone names Pentecostal and charismatic churches. Confirm the wording.
14:27–31 is paraphrased ('by two or three, in turn, with someone to interpret... prophets one at a time'); the counts come from 14:27 and 14:29.
games.original: confirm εὐσχημόνως καὶ κατὰ τάξιν (14:40) and the sound-out; trapdoor's οἰκοδομή (14:26) likewise.
